entry_json.definition: the kind of person you really are, including your character and your feelings
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Long-term stress can leave people feeling cut off from their usual self.
example_sentences: After a month of rest she was back to her old self.
Social media rewards a polished version of the self rather than the real person.

contexts.text: Long-term stress can leave people feeling cut off from their usual self.
Honestly, I didn't feel like my usual self at all that week.
The study examines how adolescents build a sense of self online.

confusables.difference: Self is a neutral noun for who you are. Selfish is a negative adjective meaning you think only about yourself.
minimal_pair: He is rediscovering his true self.

confusables.difference: Myself is a reflexive pronoun used with a verb. The self is a noun you can put 'the' or 'my' in front of.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'self' where English wants a reflexive pronoun: say "I did it myself", not "I did it self".

entry_json.definition: high in rank or position, or older than other people in a group
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Decisions of this size are normally taken by senior managers rather than by the team.
example_sentences: She was promoted to a senior role after only three years.
Senior citizens travel free on buses in most British cities.

contexts.text: Decisions of this size are normally taken by senior managers rather than by the team.
My sister is a senior nurse now, so she does a lot of the training.
Women remain under-represented in senior academic posts.

confusables.difference: Senior is about rank at work, or polite age. Elder is only about age within a family or community, and cannot follow 'more'.
minimal_pair: She is senior to me at the bank.

confusables.difference: Older simply compares age. Senior adds authority: a senior colleague may be younger than you.

entry_json.avoid: Say "senior to me", not "senior than me". Senior takes 'to', never 'than'.

entry_json.definition: showing good judgement; practical and reasonable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A sensible revision plan leaves time for sleep as well as for study.
example_sentences: It would be sensible to book the ticket before prices rise.
She gave me some very sensible advice about choosing a course.

contexts.text: A sensible revision plan leaves time for sleep as well as for study.
I think the sensible thing is to save first and travel later.
A sensible policy would combine higher fuel taxes with better public transport.

confusables.difference: Sensible means practical and wise. Sensitive means easily hurt or quick to notice feelings. Learners swap these two constantly.
minimal_pair: He is sensitive about his accent.

confusables.difference: Reasonable is about being fair or acceptable; sensible is about showing good judgement.

entry_json.avoid: Sensible does not mean 'able to feel'. "I am sensible about the noise" is wrong; you mean sensitive.

entry_json.definition: easily affected, hurt or upset; or needing to be treated with care
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Immigration is a sensitive topic, so writers should present both sides carefully.
example_sentences: My skin is sensitive to strong sunlight.
Teachers need to be sensitive to the pressure that exams put on students.

contexts.text: Immigration is a sensitive topic, so writers should present both sides carefully.
I'm quite sensitive to caffeine, so I stop drinking coffee after lunch.
Coral reefs are extremely sensitive to small rises in water temperature.

confusables.difference: Sensitive is about feeling and reacting. Sensible is about thinking clearly and acting wisely.
minimal_pair: She is sensible with her time.

confusables.difference: Touchy is informal and negative, suggesting someone is too easily offended. Sensitive is neutral and safe in writing.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'sensitive to', not 'sensitive for'. Also, praising a person as 'sensible' when you mean kind and aware is a different word.

entry_json.definition: a set of events, actions or numbers that follow one another in a particular order
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The diagram shows the sequence of stages in the recycling of glass.
example_sentences: The photographs are arranged in the sequence in which they were taken.
A short sequence of simple exercises is enough to warm up before running.

contexts.text: The diagram shows the sequence of stages in the recycling of glass.
We had to put the slides back in the right sequence before the presentation.
Figure 2 sets out the sequence of chemical reactions involved.

confusables.difference: A sequence has a fixed order that matters. A series is simply a number of similar things, ordered or not.
minimal_pair: The sequence of steps cannot be changed.
There was a series of accidents last winter.

confusables.difference: Order is the arrangement itself; a sequence is the set of items in that arrangement.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 process questions, write 'the sequence of stages', not 'the sequences' — the singular covers the whole process.

entry_json.definition: in a way that is severe or important; or in a way that shows you mean what you say
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Few governments took the warnings about air quality seriously enough.
example_sentences: He was seriously injured in a cycling accident last year.
Seriously, you should apply for that scholarship.

contexts.text: Few governments took the warnings about air quality seriously enough.
Seriously, the traffic in my city has got much worse in five years.
The findings should be taken seriously by policymakers.

confusables.difference: Severely describes how bad something is. Seriously does that too, but only seriously can mean 'genuinely, not joking'.
Badly is more informal for physical harm; seriously is safer in an essay.

entry_json.avoid: 'Seriously?' as a one-word reaction is spoken only. Keep it out of Task 2.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to work in someone else's house, cooking, cleaning or similar
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the nineteenth century, thousands of young women worked as servants in city houses.
example_sentences: The museum shows how servants lived below the main rooms of the house.
Her grandmother was a servant in a large country home.

contexts.text: In the nineteenth century, thousands of young women worked as servants in city houses.
My grandfather was a civil servant, so we moved around the country a lot.
Domestic servants formed a large share of the urban workforce in 1900.

confusables.difference: Employee is the ordinary modern word for anyone with a job. Servant now sounds historical, or means someone working in a private house.
minimal_pair: She is an employee of the bank.

confusables.difference: A civil servant works for the government, not in a private home. The two-word phrase has a completely different meaning.

entry_json.avoid: Do not call ordinary staff 'servants' in an essay — it sounds insulting. Use staff, employees or workers.

entry_json.definition: a period of time spent doing one particular activity
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most courses now include a weekly session in which students practise speaking.
example_sentences: I book a two-hour session in the library every Tuesday evening.
The training session was cancelled because the coach was ill.

contexts.text: Most courses now include a weekly session in which students practise speaking.
I usually do a short gym session before work.
Participants attended six therapy sessions over three months.

confusables.difference: A lesson is taught by someone and has content. A session is any block of time given to an activity, taught or not.
minimal_pair: I have a piano lesson on Fridays.
I did a long study session on Friday.

confusables.difference: A meeting is people discussing something; a session is time spent doing something.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'make a session'. You have, hold, attend or run a session.

entry_json.definition: the place and conditions in which something happens; or a position on a machine's controls
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Learning a language in a natural setting is very different from learning it in a classroom.
example_sentences: The hotel has a beautiful setting between the lake and the mountains.
Change the setting on the washing machine to a lower temperature.

contexts.text: Learning a language in a natural setting is very different from learning it in a classroom.
I prefer studying in a quiet setting, ideally at home.
The experiment was repeated in a laboratory setting to control for noise.

confusables.difference: Scenery is the natural view you can see. Setting is the whole situation or surroundings, and can be a hospital or an office too.
minimal_pair: The scenery on the coast is stunning.
The novel has a wartime setting.

confusables.difference: Environment is broader and often means the natural world. Setting points at one specific place and situation.

entry_json.avoid: 'Settings' in the plural usually means the controls of a device. Do not use it when you mean one place.

entry_json.definition: to make your permanent home in a place, or to end an argument by reaching agreement
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many graduates settle in the city where they studied rather than returning home.
example_sentences: The two companies settled the dispute without going to court.
My parents settled here in the 1990s and never moved again.

contexts.text: Many graduates settle in the city where they studied rather than returning home.
It took me about a month to settle in after I moved.
Migrants who settle permanently tend to send less money home over time.

confusables.difference: You solve a problem by finding an answer. You settle an argument or a claim by agreeing to stop it.
minimal_pair: They settled the dispute out of court.

confusables.difference: Move is the act of going somewhere new. Settle is staying and making a life there.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'settle to a country'. It is settle in a place, and settle down when you start a stable life.

entry_json.definition: very bad, serious or harsh
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Severe flooding forced hundreds of families to leave their homes last winter.
example_sentences: Patients with severe symptoms were treated first.
The penalties for drink-driving are severe in most countries.

contexts.text: Severe flooding forced hundreds of families to leave their homes last winter.
We had a really severe storm last year and the power went off for two days.
Severe air pollution is now the leading environmental risk to health.

confusables.difference: Serious is the general word and works everywhere. Severe is stronger and is used for weather, illness, damage and shortages.
Strict describes rules and people who enforce them. Severe describes the size of harm or punishment.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use severe for a person's character in an essay; a person is strict, not severe, about rules.

entry_json.definition: the state of being male or female
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The table gives the number of applicants by age and sex.
example_sentences: The survey asked participants to state their age, sex and occupation.
In many countries, pay still differs between the sexes.

contexts.text: The table gives the number of applicants by age and sex.
At my school the classes were mixed, so both sexes studied together.
Life expectancy differs markedly by sex in almost every country.

confusables.difference: Sex refers to biological categories. Gender refers to social roles and identity, and is the safer word in most Task 2 essays about equality.
minimal_pair: Please state your sex on the form.
The essay discusses gender roles at work.

confusables.difference: Sex is the noun; sexual is the adjective. Do not write 'sex equality' when you mean gender equality.

entry_json.avoid: This word has a second, physical meaning, so keep it to data and forms in writing and prefer 'gender' when discussing society.

entry_json.definition: connected with whether someone is male or female, or with physical attraction between people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The law prohibits sexual discrimination in recruitment and pay.
example_sentences: The company has a clear policy on sexual harassment.
Health education in schools now covers sexual health.

contexts.text: The law prohibits sexual discrimination in recruitment and pay.
We had classes on sexual health when I was about fifteen.
Legislation on sexual equality in the workplace dates from the 1970s.

confusables.difference: In modern essays 'gender equality' and 'gender roles' are far more usual than 'sexual equality'. Keep sexual for health and harassment.
minimal_pair: The clinic offers sexual health advice.

entry_json.avoid: Because the word carries a physical meaning, choose 'gender' when writing about equality at work or in education.

entry_json.definition: an area that is dark and cooler because the sun does not reach it; or a particular form of a colour
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Planting trees along wide streets provides shade and lowers summer temperatures.
example_sentences: We sat in the shade of an old tree and waited for the bus.
The walls were painted in a pale shade of green.

contexts.text: Planting trees along wide streets provides shade and lowers summer temperatures.
When it's hot I always look for a seat in the shade.
Street trees can reduce surface temperatures by providing shade during peak hours.

confusables.difference: Shade is a whole cool area out of the sun. A shadow is the dark shape one particular object makes.
minimal_pair: We ate lunch in the shade.
The tower cast a long shadow.

confusables.difference: Shade is normally uncountable when it means coolness; shadow is countable when it means a shape.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'under the shadow of a tree' when you mean sitting out of the sun. That is 'in the shade'.

entry_json.definition: the dark shape that something makes on a surface when it blocks the light
entry_json.own_context_sentence: By late afternoon the tower blocks cast long shadows across the whole square.
example_sentences: Her shadow moved along the wall as she walked past the window.
Photographers work early in the morning when the shadows are soft.

contexts.text: By late afternoon the tower blocks cast long shadows across the whole square.
The new building puts our whole garden in shadow after about four o'clock.
The scandal cast a long shadow over the government's environmental record.

confusables.difference: A shadow is a dark shape with an outline. Shade is the cool area you sit in.
minimal_pair: The tree cast a shadow on the path.
The tree gave us welcome shade.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'in the shadow' when you mean protected from the sun; use 'in the shade'.

entry_json.definition: not deep, measured from the top to the bottom; or not showing serious thought
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children swim safely at the shallow end of the pool while adults use the deep end.
example_sentences: The river is shallow enough to walk across in summer.
The essay gives a shallow account of a complicated problem.

contexts.text: Children swim safely at the shallow end of the pool while adults use the deep end.
I only swim in the shallow part because I never learned properly.
Shallow coastal waters warm faster than the open ocean.

confusables.difference: Both can mean 'lacking depth of thought', but superficial is the normal academic choice. Shallow sounds like a personal criticism.
minimal_pair: He is quite a shallow person.

confusables.difference: Low is about height from the ground. Shallow is about depth from the surface downwards.

entry_json.avoid: Do not describe a person as 'shallow' in an essay; it is a judgement, not an argument.

entry_json.definition: the bad feeling you have when you know you have done something wrong or embarrassing; or a situation you are sorry about
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many people who lose their jobs feel a sense of shame that stops them asking for help.
example_sentences: It is a shame that the old library was demolished.
He admitted the mistake without any attempt to hide his shame.

contexts.text: Many people who lose their jobs feel a sense of shame that stops them asking for help.
It's a shame the museum closes so early, because I'd love to spend longer there.
Public shame remains a powerful reason for under-reporting mental illness.

confusables.difference: Guilt is about the act: you did something wrong. Shame is about the self: you feel you are bad or exposed.
minimal_pair: He felt guilt over the lie he had told.
He felt shame at being seen there.

confusables.difference: 'It's a shame' and 'it's a pity' both mean 'that is unfortunate'. Both are conversational.

entry_json.avoid: "What a shame!" is spoken English. In Task 2 write 'unfortunately' or 'regrettably'.

entry_json.definition: having a thin edge or fine point that cuts easily; or sudden and large, of a change
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The graph shows a sharp rise in electric car sales after 2020.
example_sentences: Be careful with that knife because the blade is very sharp.
There was a sharp fall in visitor numbers during the pandemic.

contexts.text: The graph shows a sharp rise in electric car sales after 2020.
I keep one really sharp knife for vegetables and use the others for everything else.
Unemployment recorded a sharp increase in the first quarter of 2009.

confusables.difference: Both describe a fast change on a graph. Steep describes the line itself; sharp describes the change and is more common with 'rise' and 'fall'.
minimal_pair: There was a sharp fall in prices.
The line shows a steep decline.

confusables.difference: Sudden is only about speed. Sharp adds size: a sharp rise is both quick and big.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'sharp' for gradual movement on a chart; that is a gradual or steady rise.

entry_json.definition: a flat board fixed to a wall or in a cupboard, used for putting things on
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The top shelf in the library holds the reference books that cannot be borrowed.
example_sentences: I put the dictionary back on the shelf where I found it.
The shelves in the supermarket were almost empty by Sunday evening.

contexts.text: The top shelf in the library holds the reference books that cannot be borrowed.
I've got one shelf just for the books I actually reread.
Products placed at eye level on the shelf sell substantially better.

confusables.difference: A cupboard is the whole enclosed space with a door. A shelf is one flat board, inside a cupboard or on an open wall.
minimal_pair: Put the plates in the cupboard.
Put the plates on the shelf.

entry_json.avoid: The plural is irregular: shelves, not 'shelfs'.

entry_json.definition: the hard outer covering of an egg, a nut, or an animal such as a snail or crab
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Turtles are easy to identify by the pattern on the shell.
example_sentences: Crack the shell and pour the egg into the pan.
We collected shells along the beach at low tide.

contexts.text: Turtles are easy to identify by the pattern on the shell.
As a kid I used to collect shells every summer holiday.
More acidic seawater makes it harder for molluscs to form a shell.

confusables.difference: Skin is soft and flexible, on people, fruit and animals. A shell is hard and protective.
minimal_pair: Peel the skin off the orange.
Crack the shell of the nut.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'shell' for the outside of fruit — that is skin or peel.

entry_json.definition: protection from bad weather or danger, or a building that gives that protection
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Food, clean water and shelter are the first needs after any natural disaster.
example_sentences: We took shelter in a doorway until the rain stopped.
The council opened a night shelter for people sleeping on the street.

contexts.text: Food, clean water and shelter are the first needs after any natural disaster.
There's a bus shelter outside my flat, so at least you stay dry waiting.
Emergency shelter is normally the first form of aid to arrive.

confusables.difference: Housing means permanent homes and the system that supplies them. Shelter is basic, often temporary protection.
minimal_pair: The city needs more affordable housing.
The charity provides shelter for a single night.

confusables.difference: Refuge is safety from people or persecution; shelter is usually from weather or from having nowhere to sleep.

entry_json.avoid: Shelter is uncountable when it means protection: write 'provide shelter', not 'provide a shelter', unless you mean one building.

entry_json.definition: a change in position, opinion or method; or a period of work in a place that operates day and night
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There has been a clear shift towards working from home since 2020.
example_sentences: Nurses on the night shift often struggle to sleep properly.
The data show a shift in public opinion on renewable energy.

contexts.text: There has been a clear shift towards working from home since 2020.
My brother works shifts, so we hardly ever eat dinner together.
The figures indicate a gradual shift from coal to gas between 1990 and 2010.

confusables.difference: Change is the neutral word for anything becoming different. A shift is a movement in direction, usually gradual and in one clear direction.
minimal_pair: There was a change in the timetable.
There was a shift towards online study.

confusables.difference: A move is a single decision or action; a shift is a broader trend.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'a shift towards' or 'a shift in', not 'a shift of', when describing a trend.

entry_json.definition: to produce or reflect light
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Solar panels generate very little power on days when the sun does not shine.
example_sentences: The sun was shining when we arrived at the coast.
Someone shone a torch through the window.

contexts.text: Solar panels generate very little power on days when the sun does not shine.
Where I live the sun shines almost every day in summer.
The report shines a light on conditions in the garment industry.

confusables.difference: Shine is the verb, shiny is the adjective. "The floor shines" and "a shiny floor" are both right; "the floor is shine" is not.

entry_json.avoid: The past tense is shone /ʃɒn/ for light, not 'shined'. Use shined only for polishing shoes.

entry_json.definition: smooth and bright, reflecting the light
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Advertisements always show a shiny new car parked on an empty road.
example_sentences: The kitchen surfaces were shiny and completely clean.
He bought a pair of shiny black shoes for the interview.

contexts.text: Advertisements always show a shiny new car parked on an empty road.
I like phones with a matt back rather than a shiny one, because of fingerprints.
Consumers respond to shiny packaging even when the product is identical.

confusables.difference: Bright means giving out a lot of light. Shiny means reflecting light from a smooth surface.

entry_json.avoid: Shiny is an everyday adjective. In academic writing prefer 'polished' or 'reflective' for surfaces.

entry_json.definition: a strong feeling of surprise caused by something unpleasant and unexpected
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The sudden rise in energy prices came as a shock to households across Europe.
example_sentences: The news of the closure was a shock to everyone in the department.
She is still in shock after the accident.

contexts.text: The sudden rise in energy prices came as a shock to households across Europe.
Moving to a colder country was a bit of a shock at first.
An external price shock can push a fragile economy into recession.

confusables.difference: A surprise can be pleasant. A shock is nearly always unpleasant and much stronger.
minimal_pair: Her visit was a lovely surprise.
The bill was a nasty shock.

confusables.difference: Shock is the noun for the event or feeling; shocked is the adjective describing the person.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'it came as a shock', not 'it came as shock'. The countable use needs an article.

entry_json.definition: feeling upset or very surprised by something unpleasant
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Readers were shocked by how little of the plastic collected is actually recycled.
example_sentences: I was shocked to hear that the course had been cancelled.
Local residents are shocked at the scale of the flooding.

contexts.text: Readers were shocked by how little of the plastic collected is actually recycled.
I was honestly shocked at how expensive rent was when I moved there.
Respondents were shocked by the level of misinformation they encountered online.

confusables.difference: Shocked describes the person who feels it. Shocking describes the thing that causes it.
minimal_pair: I was shocked by the figures.

confusables.difference: Surprised is neutral. Shocked adds distress, so do not use it for good news.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write "the news was shocked". News is shocking; people are shocked.

entry_json.definition: to fire a gun at someone or something; or to film or photograph something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The documentary was shot over three years in six different countries.
example_sentences: The film was shot entirely on a mobile phone.
Police are trained not to shoot unless there is no alternative.

contexts.text: The documentary was shot over three years in six different countries.
A friend of mine shoots weddings at weekends to earn extra money.
Much of the footage was shot on hand-held cameras.

confusables.difference: Shoot is the verb; shot is both the past tense and a separate noun meaning a photograph or an attempt.
minimal_pair: They shoot the scenes at night.

confusables.difference: Film as a verb is neutral and general. Shoot is the industry word and suggests the practical work of recording.

entry_json.avoid: The past is shot, not 'shooted'. Also note 'shoot a film' but 'take a photograph'.

entry_json.definition: an occasion when someone is injured or killed with a gun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Countries with strict gun laws report far fewer shootings than those without.
example_sentences: The shooting took place outside a nightclub in the early hours.
Reports of a shooting in the city centre proved to be false.

contexts.text: Countries with strict gun laws report far fewer shootings than those without.
We hardly ever hear about shootings where I come from, thankfully.
The study compares shooting rates before and after the 1997 legislation.

confusables.difference: A shot is the single act of firing. A shooting is the whole violent event, usually with victims.
minimal_pair: Three people died in the shooting.

confusables.difference: Murder names the crime whatever the weapon; a shooting names the method and may not be fatal.

entry_json.avoid: 'Shooting' also means the activity of filming. Context must make clear which you mean.

entry_json.definition: an act of firing a gun; a photograph or filmed scene; or an attempt to score in sport
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The opening shot of the film shows an empty motorway at dawn.
example_sentences: He took a shot from outside the box and scored.
That is a lovely shot of the harbour at sunset.

contexts.text: The opening shot of the film shows an empty motorway at dawn.
I got a great shot of the mountains on my phone.
The director uses long shots to emphasise the emptiness of the landscape.

confusables.difference: Photo is the everyday noun for a still image. Shot suggests a deliberately composed image and covers film as well.
minimal_pair: I took a photo of the castle.
The opening shot lasts two minutes.

confusables.difference: In football a shot is the attempt; a goal is the successful result.

entry_json.avoid: 'Give it a shot' meaning 'try' is informal spoken English. Do not use it in Task 2.

entry_json.definition: nervous or uncomfortable about meeting and talking to other people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Shy students often perform well in writing but say very little in class.
example_sentences: I was too shy to ask a question in front of the whole group.
He is shy with strangers but very talkative at home.

contexts.text: Shy students often perform well in writing but say very little in class.
I used to be really shy, but working in a shop changed that.
Shy learners benefit from small-group discussion rather than whole-class questioning.

confusables.difference: Quiet describes how much someone speaks. Shy explains why: they feel nervous with people.
Modest means not boasting about your achievements; shy is about social nervousness.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'I have shy'. Shy is an adjective: 'I am shy'.

entry_json.definition: the ability to see; or something that you see, especially something worth seeing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Regular screen use over long hours can gradually damage a person's sight.
example_sentences: She lost her sight in one eye after the illness.
The old harbour at sunset is a wonderful sight.

contexts.text: Regular screen use over long hours can gradually damage a person's sight.
The best sight in my city is definitely the view from the hill.
Untreated diabetes remains a leading cause of loss of sight worldwide.

confusables.difference: A view is what you can see from a particular place. A sight is a thing worth looking at, wherever you stand.
minimal_pair: The room has a view of the sea.
The cathedral is an impressive sight.

confusables.difference: Site and sight sound identical. A site is a place where something is built or happens.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse the spelling with 'site' (a place) or 'cite' (to quote a source).

entry_json.definition: a movement, sound or light that gives information or an instruction; or the radio waves that carry a phone or television transmission
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A rise in interest rates is usually read as a signal that inflation is a concern.
example_sentences: The mobile signal disappears completely once the train enters the tunnel.
The driver gave a clear signal before turning left.

contexts.text: A rise in interest rates is usually read as a signal that inflation is a concern.
The signal in my building is terrible, so I have to stand by the window.
Falling applications send a signal that the sector is losing its appeal.

confusables.difference: A sign is a board with information, or evidence that something is true. A signal is deliberately sent to communicate.
minimal_pair: There is a sign at the entrance.
She gave a signal to start.

confusables.difference: A symbol stands for an idea permanently; a signal is sent at one moment.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'the signal is weak' about a person's message; that is 'the message is unclear'.

entry_json.definition: large or important enough to have an effect or to be worth attention
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There has been a significant reduction in the number of people smoking daily.
example_sentences: The city has made significant progress in reducing waste.
Age was the only significant factor in the results.

contexts.text: There has been a significant reduction in the number of people smoking daily.
There's been a significant change in how people my age shop.
The difference between the two groups was statistically significant.

confusables.difference: Considerable is only about size — a considerable amount. Significant adds importance or meaning, and in research it means 'unlikely to be chance'.
minimal_pair: There was a considerable amount of rain.
The rainfall had a significant effect on the harvest.

confusables.difference: Important is the general word. Significant sounds more measured and is the safer choice in a data essay.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'significant' simply to mean 'big' when describing a chart. If you only mean size, 'considerable' or 'substantial' is more accurate.

entry_json.definition: in a way that is large enough to be important or noticeable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: House prices rose significantly faster than wages between 2000 and 2020.
example_sentences: Air quality has improved significantly since the ban on coal fires.
The two groups did not differ significantly in their test scores.

contexts.text: House prices rose significantly faster than wages between 2000 and 2020.
My spending on transport has gone up significantly this year.
Participation rates were significantly higher among urban respondents.

confusables.difference: Considerably reports size only. Significantly implies the difference matters, and in statistics it has a technical meaning.
minimal_pair: Prices rose significantly faster than incomes.

confusables.difference: Dramatically is stronger and more emotional; significantly is the neutral academic choice.

entry_json.avoid: Do not overuse 'significantly' in Task 1 as a synonym for 'a lot'. Vary it with 'considerably', 'markedly' and 'sharply'.

entry_json.definition: a complete lack of sound or speech
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Libraries remain one of the few public places where silence is expected.
example_sentences: There was a long silence before anyone answered the question.
The class worked in silence for twenty minutes.

contexts.text: Libraries remain one of the few public places where silence is expected.
I can only study in complete silence, so cafés are hopeless for me.
The government's silence on the report was widely criticised.

example_sentences: Her tone made it clear that the discussion was over.
The report adopts a cautious tone throughout.

contexts.text: An email written in the wrong tone can undo weeks of careful negotiation.
I could tell from his tone that something was wrong.
The editorial adopts a noticeably more critical tone after 2015.

confusables.difference: Voice is the sound itself. Tone is the attitude that the sound or the writing conveys.
Style is how something is written overall; tone is the attitude it expresses.

entry_json.avoid: In Writing Task 1 of the General paper, 'tone' means formality. Match it to the reader, and keep it consistent.

entry_json.definition: the soft part inside the mouth used for tasting and speaking; or a language
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Learners often find that sounds absent from their mother tongue are the hardest to produce.
example_sentences: I burned my tongue on the coffee.
She speaks three languages, but Arabic is her mother tongue.

contexts.text: Learners often find that sounds absent from their mother tongue are the hardest to produce.
My mother tongue is Tamil, though I studied mostly in English.
Instruction in the mother tongue improves early literacy outcomes.

confusables.difference: Language is the ordinary word. Tongue is used mainly in the fixed phrase 'mother tongue' or in literary writing.

entry_json.avoid: Note the pronunciation: /tʌŋ/, rhyming with 'young'. The 'ue' is silent.

entry_json.definition: including everything; complete
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Total household waste fell by a fifth over the ten-year period.
example_sentences: The total cost of the project came to two million pounds.
The building was a total loss after the fire.

contexts.text: Total household waste fell by a fifth over the ten-year period.
The total came to about forty pounds each, which was more than I expected.
Total energy consumption rose steadily until 2008 and then levelled off.

confusables.difference: Whole describes one complete thing. Total adds up several separate amounts.
minimal_pair: The total number of books is 300.

confusables.difference: Overall takes everything into account when judging; total is arithmetic.

entry_json.avoid: Write 'in total', not 'in the total', when summing figures in Task 1.

entry_json.definition: completely; in every way
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The two proposals rest on totally different assumptions about future demand.
example_sentences: I totally forgot about the appointment.
The old system was totally replaced in 2019.

contexts.text: The two proposals rest on totally different assumptions about future demand.
I totally agree with you on that.
The two data sets are not totally comparable, since the definitions changed.

confusables.difference: Completely is the neutral written choice. Totally is more emphatic and sounds informal in an essay.
Entirely is the most formal of the three and is the safest in Task 2.

entry_json.avoid: 'Totally!' as a one-word agreement is casual speech. In Task 2 use 'entirely' or 'completely'.

entry_json.definition: difficult to do or deal with; or strong and not easily broken or damaged
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Tough enforcement, rather than new laws, is usually what changes driver behaviour.
example_sentences: The first year of the course was tough, but I got through it.
These boots are tough enough for winter walking.

contexts.text: Tough enforcement, rather than new laws, is usually what changes driver behaviour.
It was a tough year, honestly, but I learned a lot.
Tougher penalties alone have rarely reduced reoffending rates.

confusables.difference: Difficult is the neutral written word. Tough is more informal and adds the sense of needing endurance.
Hard covers both difficulty and physical firmness; tough emphasises resistance and durability.

entry_json.avoid: Pronounce it /tʌf/, rhyming with 'stuff'. The 'gh' is an f sound.

entry_json.definition: the buying and selling of goods and services, especially between countries
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Trade between neighbouring countries usually grows fastest when transport links improve.
example_sentences: The port handles most of the country's trade with Asia.
Restrictions on trade were lifted in 2015.

contexts.text: Trade between neighbouring countries usually grows fastest when transport links improve.
My uncle works in the import trade, so he travels constantly.
Trade in manufactured goods grew fourfold between 1990 and 2010.

confusables.difference: Business is commercial activity in general, or one company. Trade is specifically buying and selling, especially across borders.
Commerce is the formal near-synonym; trade is the more usual word in essays and in data.

entry_json.avoid: Trade is uncountable in this sense. Write 'trade increased', not 'trades increased'.

entry_json.definition: to move someone or something from one place, job or account to another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students who transfer between institutions often lose credit for work already completed.
example_sentences: The money was transferred to my account the same day.
She transferred to the Manchester office last autumn.

contexts.text: Students who transfer between institutions often lose credit for work already completed.
I transferred the deposit online and it arrived within an hour.
Skills acquired in one language frequently transfer to another.

confusables.difference: Move is the everyday word for changing position. Transfer is formal and implies an official process or an account.
minimal_pair: I moved to a new flat.
I transferred to a new department.

confusables.difference: Transfer means to move something. Transform means to change what it is. The two are often confused.

entry_json.avoid: Stress the verb on the last syllable, /trænsˈfɜː(r)/. The noun 'a transfer' is stressed on the first.

entry_json.definition: to change something completely, usually so that it is better
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap sensors have transformed the way cities manage traffic and waste.
example_sentences: The internet transformed how research is carried out.
The old warehouse has been transformed into a public library.

contexts.text: Cheap sensors have transformed the way cities manage traffic and waste.
Working from home has completely transformed my daily routine.
Mechanisation transformed agricultural employment within a single generation.

confusables.difference: Change is neutral and can be small. Transform means a complete change of character, and is far stronger.
Transform changes what something is; transfer moves it somewhere else.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'transform X into Y', not 'transform X to Y'.

entry_json.definition: the process of changing from one state or system to another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The transition from coal to renewables is technically possible and politically difficult.
example_sentences: The transition from school to work is harder than it used to be.
A smooth transition to the new software took eighteen months.

contexts.text: The transition from coal to renewables is technically possible and politically difficult.
The transition to living alone was harder than I expected.
The energy transition will require substantial investment in grid capacity.

confusables.difference: Change is the event. A transition is the whole process of moving between two states, and takes time.
minimal_pair: There was a change of government.

confusables.difference: A shift is a movement in direction, often unplanned. A transition is usually a managed process with a start and an end.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'transition to' or 'transition from X to Y'. Not 'transition into' in formal writing.

entry_json.definition: to change words from one language into another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Legal documents are expensive to translate because a single error can change their meaning.
example_sentences: The novel has been translated into over thirty languages.
Could you translate this sentence for me?

contexts.text: Legal documents are expensive to translate because a single error can change their meaning.
I sometimes translate for my parents when they go to the doctor.
Research funding rarely translates directly into commercial products.

confusables.difference: Interpret is done aloud, in real time, between speakers. Translate is done with written text.
Explain makes meaning clearer in the same language; translate moves it into another.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'translate from Spanish into English'. Do not write 'translate to English' in careful writing.

entry_json.definition: the process of changing words into another language, or the text that results
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Automatic translation is good enough for a menu and dangerous for a contract.
example_sentences: I read the novel in translation because my Russian is not good enough.
The translation loses some of the humour of the original.

contexts.text: Automatic translation is good enough for a menu and dangerous for a contract.
I use an app for translation when I travel, and it usually works.
Machine translation has reduced the cost of multilingual publishing considerably.

confusables.difference: Interpretation is spoken, or means the meaning you take from something. Translation is the written version in another language.
minimal_pair: Her interpretation of the data is questionable.
Her translation of the poem is beautiful.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'do a translation of' in formal English; 'translate' as a verb is cleaner.

entry_json.definition: to behave towards someone in a particular way; or to give medical care to someone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Employers who treat part-time staff as temporary lose them within a year.
example_sentences: The doctor treated her for a chest infection.
He treats everyone in the team with the same respect.

contexts.text: Employers who treat part-time staff as temporary lose them within a year.
My old boss treated everyone fairly, which is rarer than it should be.
The condition can now be treated effectively with a single course of drugs.

confusables.difference: Cure means the illness is removed completely. Treat means giving care, which may or may not cure.
minimal_pair: The clinic treats hundreds of patients a week.

confusables.difference: Handle is about dealing with a situation. Treat is about how you behave towards a person.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'treat someone for an illness', not 'treat someone from an illness'.

entry_json.definition: medical care given to a patient; or the way someone is dealt with
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Early treatment costs far less than the emergency care it prevents.
example_sentences: The treatment lasted six weeks and worked very well.
Staff complained about their treatment by the new management.

contexts.text: Early treatment costs far less than the emergency care it prevents.
The treatment was free, which made an enormous difference to my family.
Equal treatment before the law is a founding principle of the system.

confusables.difference: A cure ends the illness. A treatment manages it, and may need to continue indefinitely.
Therapy usually means repeated sessions; treatment covers drugs and surgery as well.

entry_json.avoid: Treatment is uncountable when it means care in general: 'receive treatment', not 'receive a treatment'.

entry_json.definition: a general direction in which a situation is changing or developing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The overall trend is upward, although there are two brief falls in the middle of the period.
example_sentences: There is a clear trend towards later marriage across Europe.
The graph shows a downward trend in newspaper sales.

contexts.text: The overall trend is upward, although there are two brief falls in the middle of the period.
There's a real trend towards working from home in my industry.
The trend towards urban living has accelerated since 2000.

confusables.difference: A tendency is what an individual or group is inclined to do. A trend is a measurable movement in data over time.
minimal_pair: He has a tendency to interrupt.
The data show an upward trend.

confusables.difference: A fashion is a short-lived popular style. A trend in Task 1 means the direction of the figures.

entry_json.avoid: Task 1 requires 'the overall trend'. Write 'a trend towards X', not 'a trend of X'.

entry_json.definition: a test of something new to see how well it works; or a legal process in a court
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A drug that performs well in a small trial may still fail when it reaches the public.
example_sentences: The scheme is being tested in a two-year trial in four cities.
The trial lasted three weeks and ended in an acquittal.

contexts.text: A drug that performs well in a small trial may still fail when it reaches the public.
My neighbour took part in a clinical trial last year.
The randomised controlled trial included over four thousand participants.

confusables.difference: An experiment tests a scientific idea under controlled conditions. A trial tests whether something works in practice, often on people.
minimal_pair: The vaccine trial ran for two years.

confusables.difference: A test is any single check. A trial is an organised period of testing.

entry_json.avoid: 'Trial and error' is a fixed phrase and takes no article.

entry_json.definition: a clever method of doing something; or an action intended to deceive someone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The trick with Listening is to read the questions before the recording starts.
example_sentences: He showed me a simple trick for remembering names.
The advertisement was a trick to collect personal data.

contexts.text: The trick with Listening is to read the questions before the recording starts.
My friend taught me a trick for peeling garlic quickly.
Some sites use design tricks that make cancelling deliberately difficult.

confusables.difference: Technique is the formal word for a skilled method. Trick is informal and suggests a shortcut.
minimal_pair: The surgeon uses a new technique.
There is a trick to opening it.

confusables.difference: A skill takes practice to acquire; a trick is a shortcut anyone can be told.

entry_json.avoid: Trick is informal. In Task 2 write 'strategy', 'technique' or 'approach'.

entry_json.definition: belonging to or typical of the hot, wet regions near the equator
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Tropical forests store more carbon per hectare than any other land ecosystem.
example_sentences: Tropical storms have become more intense over the last thirty years.
The island has a tropical climate with heavy summer rain.

contexts.text: Tropical forests store more carbon per hectare than any other land ecosystem.
I grew up in a tropical climate, so British winters were a shock.
Tropical deforestation accounts for a substantial share of global emissions.

confusables.difference: Humid describes air with a lot of water in it, anywhere in the world. Tropical describes a whole climate zone near the equator.
minimal_pair: The region has a tropical climate.

confusables.difference: Exotic means unfamiliar and foreign, which is a judgement. Tropical is a geographical fact.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'tropical' loosely to mean 'hot'. A desert is hot but not tropical.

entry_json.definition: really; in a way that is genuine and not just claimed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Very few products are truly recyclable once they have been mixed with other materials.
example_sentences: This is a truly international university, with students from ninety countries.
I am truly grateful for everything you have done.

contexts.text: Very few products are truly recyclable once they have been mixed with other materials.
It was a truly memorable trip, one of the best I've had.
Few of the schemes described are truly self-financing.

confusables.difference: Really is the everyday spoken intensifier. Truly is stronger and suggests genuineness rather than degree.
minimal_pair: It was a truly original piece of work.

confusables.difference: Actually corrects a mistaken belief; truly emphasises that something genuinely is what it claims.

entry_json.avoid: Note the spelling: no 'e'. It is truly, not 'truely'.

entry_json.definition: to believe that someone is honest and reliable, or that something is safe and true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Voters no longer trust official figures if they cannot see how they were produced.
example_sentences: I would not trust that website for medical information.
You can trust her to keep her word.

contexts.text: Voters no longer trust official figures if they cannot see how they were produced.
I trust my doctor, but I still look things up afterwards.
Citizens who trust public institutions comply with regulations more readily.

confusables.difference: Believe is about accepting a statement as true. Trust is about relying on a person or source over time.
Rely on is about depending practically; trust is about confidence in honesty.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'trust someone', with no preposition. 'Trust in' exists but is formal and slightly religious.

entry_json.definition: the real facts about a situation, rather than what people claim
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Journalists cannot check every claim, and that is why the truth spreads more slowly than rumour.
example_sentences: Nobody knows the full truth about what happened that night.
There is some truth in the argument, even if it is exaggerated.

contexts.text: Journalists cannot check every claim, and that is why the truth spreads more slowly than rumour.
To tell you the truth, I've never really enjoyed team sports.
Establishing the truth of a claim requires evidence that can be independently checked.

confusables.difference: A fact is one specific piece of verified information. Truth is the whole accurate picture.
Reality is how things actually are; truth is the accurate account of them.

entry_json.avoid: 'To tell you the truth' is a spoken filler. Do not use it in Task 2.

entry_json.definition: a long hollow pipe for liquid or gas, or a container of soft material you squeeze
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Water is carried across the city in tubes laid more than a century ago.
example_sentences: I bought a tube of toothpaste and some soap.
The gas travels through a narrow tube into the burner.

contexts.text: Water is carried across the city in tubes laid more than a century ago.
I take the tube to work, which takes about half an hour.
Samples were sealed in test tubes and stored at four degrees.

confusables.difference: A pipe is usually rigid and fixed, carrying water or gas in a building. A tube is often flexible or small.
minimal_pair: The pipe under the sink burst.
Blood is drawn into a small tube.

confusables.difference: A bottle is rigid with a neck; a tube is squeezed and collapses.

entry_json.avoid: 'The Tube' with a capital letter means the London Underground. Elsewhere in Britain the underground railway has other names.

entry_json.definition: a series of musical notes that is pleasant and easy to remember
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A memorable tune does more for a public health campaign than any amount of text.
example_sentences: I cannot remember the words, but the tune has stayed with me all day.
She hummed a tune while she worked.

contexts.text: A memorable tune does more for a public health campaign than any amount of text.
There's one tune from my childhood that I still hear everywhere.
Advertisers use a repeated tune to make a brand easier to recall.

confusables.difference: A song has words. A tune is the melody alone, which may have no words at all.
Melody is the technical musical term; tune is the everyday word.

entry_json.avoid: 'In tune' means at the right pitch. Do not confuse it with 'in time', which is about rhythm.

entry_json.definition: a passage built underground or through a hill for a road, railway or people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A rail tunnel costs several times more per kilometre than track laid on the surface.
example_sentences: The train goes through a long tunnel just before the border.
Work on the new tunnel will take at least six years.

contexts.text: A rail tunnel costs several times more per kilometre than track laid on the surface.
The signal always drops when we go through the tunnel.
The tunnel reduced journey times between the two cities by an hour.

confusables.difference: A bridge goes over an obstacle; a tunnel goes under or through it.
minimal_pair: They built a bridge over the river.
They dug a tunnel under the river.

confusables.difference: An underpass is a short pedestrian passage under a road; a tunnel is much longer.

entry_json.avoid: Double the l in British English: tunnelled, tunnelling.

entry_json.definition: in most cases; in the way that is usual for a person, group or thing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Households typically spend about a third of their income on housing.
example_sentences: A consultation typically lasts around ten minutes.
Typically, applications rise sharply in the final week.

contexts.text: Households typically spend about a third of their income on housing.
I typically get up at six, even at the weekend.
Symptoms typically appear between two and five days after exposure.

confusables.difference: Usually is the everyday word for frequency. Typically suggests this is the standard pattern, and is more common in reports.
Generally means in most respects; typically means in the standard case.

entry_json.avoid: Do not overuse 'typically' as a synonym for 'always'. It allows exceptions.

entry_json.definition: the thick rubber ring fitted around the wheel of a vehicle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Worn tyres are a factor in a significant proportion of wet-weather accidents.
example_sentences: I had a flat tyre on the way to the station.
Check your tyres before a long journey.

contexts.text: Worn tyres are a factor in a significant proportion of wet-weather accidents.
I got a flat tyre on my bike and had to walk the rest of the way.
Tyre particles are now recognised as a major source of microplastic pollution.

confusables.difference: The wheel is the metal disc that turns. The tyre is the rubber fitted around it.
'Tire' is the American spelling of this noun, and also a British verb meaning to become tired.

entry_json.avoid: With British examiners write 'tyre', not 'tire'.

entry_json.definition: unpleasant to look at
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap post-war blocks were widely called ugly, and many are now protected buildings.
example_sentences: The new car park is an ugly addition to a beautiful street.
Nobody wants an ugly building opposite their window.

contexts.text: Cheap post-war blocks were widely called ugly, and many are now protected buildings.
I think the new shopping centre is genuinely ugly, but my friends disagree.
Public opposition to the design centred on claims that it was ugly and out of scale.

confusables.difference: Unattractive is milder and more polite, and is the better choice in writing. Ugly is blunt.
Plain means simple and undecorated, which is not the same as unpleasant to look at.

entry_json.avoid: Never describe a person as ugly in an essay. Even about buildings, 'unattractive' sounds more measured.

entry_json.definition: in the end, after everything else has been considered; or finally, after a long process
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Ultimately, the success of any recycling scheme depends on how easy it is to use.
example_sentences: The proposal was ultimately rejected by the council.
Ultimately it is the taxpayer who pays for these subsidies.

contexts.text: Ultimately, the success of any recycling scheme depends on how easy it is to use.
Ultimately I decided to stay, mostly because of my family.
Ultimately the policy shifted costs from the state to individual households.

confusables.difference: Finally is about the last item in a sequence or the end of a wait. Ultimately is about the fundamental point once everything is weighed.
minimal_pair: Ultimately, the decision rests with parliament.

confusables.difference: Eventually is about time passing before something happens; ultimately is about the underlying conclusion.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'ultimately' to introduce your last body paragraph. That is 'finally'.

entry_json.definition: not having the ability, opportunity or permission to do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Patients who are unable to travel are the ones least likely to receive follow-up care.
example_sentences: I was unable to attend the meeting because of a delayed flight.
Many households are unable to afford the increase in rent.

contexts.text: Patients who are unable to travel are the ones least likely to receive follow-up care.
I was unable to get a ticket, so I watched it at home.
A third of respondents were unable to name a single local service.

confusables.difference: Cannot is the ordinary way to say this and is fine in speech and writing. Unable is more formal and is followed by 'to'.
Disabled describes a long-term condition. Unable describes a temporary or specific inability.

entry_json.avoid: Unable is always followed by 'to' plus a verb. 'Unable of doing' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: not physically relaxed or pleasant; or feeling embarrassed or worried
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Long flights in economy class are uncomfortable in a way that no amount of planning solves.
example_sentences: The chairs in the lecture hall are extremely uncomfortable.
I felt uncomfortable being asked about my salary.

contexts.text: Long flights in economy class are uncomfortable in a way that no amount of planning solves.
The bus is cheap but really uncomfortable on a long journey.
Participants reported feeling uncomfortable when asked about household income.

confusables.difference: Unpleasant is about something being nasty in itself. Uncomfortable is about how it makes you feel physically or socially.
Awkward describes a socially difficult situation; uncomfortable describes the feeling it produces.

entry_json.avoid: Note the pronunciation: /ʌnˈkʌmftəbl/, four syllables, not 'un-com-for-ta-ble'.

entry_json.definition: not awake and not aware of what is happening; or done without realising it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Unconscious bias in recruitment is difficult to prove and easy to demonstrate in experiments.
example_sentences: He was unconscious for several minutes after the fall.
Many of our daily choices are largely unconscious.

contexts.text: Unconscious bias in recruitment is difficult to prove and easy to demonstrate in experiments.
He was unconscious when the ambulance arrived, but he recovered completely.
Unconscious associations shape hiring decisions even among trained assessors.

confusables.difference: Asleep is normal rest that you wake from naturally. Unconscious is a medical state you cannot be woken from.
Subconscious refers to mental processes just below awareness. Unconscious is used both medically and for bias.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'he fell unconscious asleep'. The two words describe different states.

entry_json.definition: clothes worn next to the skin under other clothes
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap underwear made from synthetic fibres sheds plastic every time it is washed.
example_sentences: Pack enough underwear for a week.
The shop sells underwear and socks on the ground floor.

contexts.text: Cheap underwear made from synthetic fibres sheds plastic every time it is washed.
I always forget to pack enough underwear when I travel.
Synthetic underwear contributes to microfibre release during laundering.

confusables.difference: Clothes is everything you wear. Underwear is only the layer worn next to the skin.

entry_json.avoid: Underwear is uncountable. Write 'some underwear' or 'two pairs of underwear', never 'underwears'.

entry_json.definition: without a paid job, although wanting to work
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Young people who are unemployed for more than a year earn less for decades afterwards.
example_sentences: He was unemployed for eight months after the factory closed.
The scheme offers free training to unemployed adults.

contexts.text: Young people who are unemployed for more than a year earn less for decades afterwards.
I was unemployed for about six months and it was a difficult time.
The proportion of unemployed graduates fell steadily after 2013.

confusables.difference: Jobless is the journalistic word and appears in headlines. Unemployed is the standard term in reports and essays.
Retired people have stopped working by choice or age; the unemployed are looking for work.

entry_json.avoid: 'The unemployed' takes a plural verb: 'the unemployed are entitled to support'.

entry_json.definition: the situation in which people who want jobs cannot find them, or the number of such people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Unemployment fell steadily from 2013 onwards, reaching its lowest level in the final year shown.
example_sentences: Youth unemployment remains far higher than the national average.
The region suffered high unemployment throughout the 1980s.

contexts.text: Unemployment fell steadily from 2013 onwards, reaching its lowest level in the final year shown.
Unemployment is quite high in my hometown, which is why people leave.
Unemployment among the under-25s peaked at twenty-two per cent in 2012.

confusables.difference: Redundancy is losing a specific job because it no longer exists. Unemployment is the state of having no job at all.
minimal_pair: He was made redundant in March.

entry_json.avoid: Unemployment is uncountable. Write 'high unemployment', never 'a high unemployment'.

entry_json.definition: surprising, because you did not think it would happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The most useful finding was unexpected: the cheapest option also produced the best results.
example_sentences: An unexpected delay meant we missed the connection.
The results were unexpected and the study was repeated.

contexts.text: The most useful finding was unexpected: the cheapest option also produced the best results.
I had an unexpected phone call from an old colleague last week.
An unexpected fall in demand undermined the original cost projections.

confusables.difference: Sudden is about speed with no warning. Unexpected is about surprise, and something slow can still be unexpected.
Surprising describes something that causes surprise; unexpected states that it was not predicted.

entry_json.avoid: Note the stress: /ˌʌnɪkˈspektɪd/, with the main stress on 'spec'.

entry_json.definition: not treating people equally or according to what is right
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is unfair to judge schools on results alone when their intakes differ so much.
example_sentences: Many workers feel that the new shift system is unfair.
The test gives an unfair advantage to students who can pay for coaching.

contexts.text: It is unfair to judge schools on results alone when their intakes differ so much.
I thought it was unfair that only full-time staff got the bonus.
Critics argue that the funding formula is unfair to rural authorities.

confusables.difference: Unjust is stronger and usually concerns law and morality. Unfair covers everyday inequality of treatment.
Unequal states a difference in amount; unfair judges that difference to be wrong.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'unfair to someone' or 'unfair on someone'. Not 'unfair for someone' when you mean badly treated.

entry_json.definition: an organisation of workers formed to protect their rights; or the joining together of states or groups
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Membership of a trade union has fallen in almost every developed economy since 1980.
example_sentences: The union negotiated a four per cent pay rise.
The European Union has twenty-seven member states.

contexts.text: Membership of a trade union has fallen in almost every developed economy since 1980.
I joined the union in my first week and I've never regretted it.
Union density correlates closely with lower income inequality.

confusables.difference: An association is any organised group with shared interests. A union specifically represents workers in bargaining with employers.

entry_json.avoid: Note the article: 'a union', not 'an union'. The word begins with a consonant sound, /j/.

entry_json.definition: being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Every city claims a unique character, but the evidence for it is often thin.
example_sentences: Each fingerprint is unique to the individual.
The building is unique in Europe.

contexts.text: Every city claims a unique character, but the evidence for it is often thin.
The atmosphere at that festival is unique — I've never felt anything like it.
The species is unique to a single valley in the north of the island.

confusables.difference: Special means unusually good or important. Unique means there is literally no other one, which is a much stronger claim.
Rare means very few exist; unique means exactly one does.

entry_json.avoid: Unique is absolute. Do not write 'very unique' or 'more unique'. Use 'truly unique' if you need emphasis.

entry_json.definition: everything that exists, including all the stars, planets and space between them
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Public funding for research into the universe competes directly with funding for health.
example_sentences: The universe is thought to be around 13.8 billion years old.
New telescopes let us see parts of the universe that were invisible a decade ago.

contexts.text: Public funding for research into the universe competes directly with funding for health.
I find documentaries about the universe strangely relaxing.
Observations suggest that the expansion of the universe is accelerating.

confusables.difference: World normally means the earth and the people on it. Universe means everything that physically exists.
