entry_json.own_context_sentence: A weather warning issued a day in advance saves more lives than any rescue service.
example_sentences: The council issued a flood warning on Thursday evening.
He was given a written warning for repeated lateness.

contexts.text: A weather warning issued a day in advance saves more lives than any rescue service.
We got a text warning about the storm the night before it hit.
Early warning systems have reduced deaths from cyclones by an order of magnitude.

confusables.difference: A notice is any announcement, often routine. A warning specifically concerns danger or consequences.
minimal_pair: There is a notice on the door.
There is a warning on the packet.

confusables.difference: An alert is urgent and immediate; a warning may be about a longer-term risk.

entry_json.avoid: You 'issue' or 'give' a warning. Do not write 'make a warning'.

entry_json.definition: materials that are thrown away because they are no longer needed; or the wrong use of time or money
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Household waste per person has fallen slightly since 2010, while packaging has not.
example_sentences: The city sends less than half its waste to landfill.
Meetings without an agenda are a waste of everyone's time.

contexts.text: Household waste per person has fallen slightly since 2010, while packaging has not.
I think fast fashion is a complete waste of money and materials.
Food waste accounts for roughly a tenth of global greenhouse gas emissions.

confusables.difference: Rubbish is the everyday British word for what you throw away at home. Waste is the technical term used in policy and data.
Litter is rubbish dropped in a public place; waste is the whole category.

entry_json.avoid: Waste is uncountable as material: 'less waste', not 'fewer wastes'.

entry_json.definition: a fault or a lack of strength in a person, plan or system
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main weakness of the study is that it relies entirely on what people say they eat.
example_sentences: Candidates are usually asked to describe their greatest weakness.
The report identifies several weaknesses in the current system.

contexts.text: The main weakness of the study is that it relies entirely on what people say they eat.
My biggest weakness at work is that I take on too much.
A key weakness of the methodology is the absence of a control group.

confusables.difference: A fault is a specific defect that can often be fixed. A weakness is a general lack of strength or a limitation.
minimal_pair: There is a fault in the wiring.
The plan has one serious weakness.

confusables.difference: A disadvantage is a drawback compared with alternatives; a weakness is an internal flaw.

entry_json.avoid: 'A weakness for chocolate' means you cannot resist it. That is a different, informal sense.

entry_json.definition: a large amount of money and property owned by a person or country
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wealth is distributed far more unequally than income in almost every country studied.
example_sentences: The country's wealth comes largely from oil.
Much of the family's wealth was inherited rather than earned.

contexts.text: Wealth is distributed far more unequally than income in almost every country studied.
There's a huge gap in wealth between the two sides of my city.
The top one per cent hold a disproportionate share of national wealth.

confusables.difference: Income is money coming in each month or year. Wealth is what you already own. A person can have high income and no wealth.
minimal_pair: Her wealth is mostly in property.

confusables.difference: Money is the everyday word. Wealth is the accumulated total of assets and is the term used in economics.

entry_json.avoid: Wealth is uncountable. Write 'great wealth', never 'a wealth' unless you mean 'a wealth of experience'.

entry_json.definition: having a lot of money and property; rich
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wealthy households cut their energy use least when prices rise, because the bill matters less.
example_sentences: The area attracts wealthy buyers from overseas.
Wealthy countries produce far more waste per person.

contexts.text: Wealthy households cut their energy use least when prices rise, because the bill matters less.
The part of town I grew up in was never wealthy, but it was safe.
Wealthy nations account for a disproportionate share of historical emissions.

confusables.difference: Rich is the everyday word and is fine in speech. Wealthy sounds more measured and is preferred in formal writing.
minimal_pair: The wealthy nations of the north.

confusables.difference: Affluent usually describes areas and societies rather than individuals, and suggests comfortable rather than enormous wealth.

entry_json.avoid: 'Rich' also describes food and colour. In an essay about money, 'wealthy' is less ambiguous.

entry_json.definition: an object used for fighting or attacking, such as a gun or a knife
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Countries that restrict access to weapons report far lower rates of fatal assault.
example_sentences: Police found no weapon at the scene.
Carrying a weapon in public is illegal in most European countries.

contexts.text: Countries that restrict access to weapons report far lower rates of fatal assault.
Where I'm from, almost nobody carries a weapon of any kind.
Legislation restricting the sale of weapons was introduced in 1996.

confusables.difference: Arms is used for military equipment and international trade. Weapon is the ordinary word for an individual object.
minimal_pair: The arms trade is worth billions.

confusables.difference: A tool is for work; a weapon is for fighting, though a tool can be used as one.

entry_json.avoid: Note the pronunciation: /ˈwepən/, with a short e. The 'ea' is not /iː/.

entry_json.definition: to have a particular weight; or to measure how heavy something is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Airlines weigh hand luggage more strictly than they used to, which changes how people pack.
example_sentences: The parcel weighs just under two kilograms.
Weigh the flour before you add the water.

contexts.text: Airlines weigh hand luggage more strictly than they used to, which changes how people pack.
I weigh my suitcase at home now because of the charges.
Samples were weighed before and after drying.

confusables.difference: Weigh is the verb; weight is the noun. "What is your weight?" and "How much do you weigh?" are both correct.
Weigh and way sound identical. Only weigh has the gh.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'it weights two kilos'. The verb is weigh.

entry_json.definition: in or from the west of a country or region; or connected with Europe and North America
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Western diets are unusually high in processed food, and the health effects are now well documented.
example_sentences: The western coast receives most of the rainfall.
Western companies were slow to enter the market.

contexts.text: Western diets are unusually high in processed food, and the health effects are now well documented.
I live in the western part of the city, near the river.
Western consumption patterns are increasingly replicated in emerging economies.

confusables.difference: West is the noun and direction. Western is the adjective describing an area or a culture.
Capitalise Western when it means the culture of Europe and North America; lower case for compass direction.

entry_json.avoid: 'The West' as a cultural bloc is a broad generalisation. In Task 2, name specific countries where you can.

entry_json.definition: at any time that; every time that
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Whenever fuel prices rise, public transport use increases within a few weeks.
example_sentences: Come and see me whenever you have a question.
Whenever I try to book, the site crashes.

contexts.text: Whenever fuel prices rise, public transport use increases within a few weeks.
I walk to work whenever the weather allows.
Data were collected whenever a new cohort entered the programme.

confusables.difference: When refers to one particular time. Whenever means every time, or at any time you like.
minimal_pair: Call me whenever you need help.

confusables.difference: Whenever is about time; wherever is about place.

entry_json.avoid: After whenever, use the present tense for future meaning: 'whenever he arrives', not 'whenever he will arrive'.

entry_json.definition: used to compare two facts that contrast with each other
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Spending on health rose steadily, whereas spending on housing fell in every year shown.
example_sentences: The north of the country is industrial, whereas the south is largely agricultural.
Men in the survey cited pay, whereas women cited flexibility.

contexts.text: Spending on health rose steadily, whereas spending on housing fell in every year shown.
I like cooking, whereas my brother eats out almost every night.
Urban participation rose, whereas rural participation remained flat.

confusables.difference: While can mean the same, but it also means 'during the time that', so it is ambiguous. Whereas only ever signals contrast.
However starts a new sentence. Whereas joins two clauses inside one sentence.

entry_json.avoid: Whereas is a conjunction, not a linking adverb. Do not start a new sentence with it in Task 1.

entry_json.definition: in or to any place that; in every place that
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wherever public transport is cheap and frequent, car ownership falls.
example_sentences: Sit wherever you like.
Wherever the disease appeared, the same pattern of spread was observed.

contexts.text: Wherever public transport is cheap and frequent, car ownership falls.
I take my laptop wherever I go, which is probably unhealthy.
Wherever data were unavailable, national estimates were substituted.

confusables.difference: Where refers to one particular place. Wherever means any or every place.
minimal_pair: I can work wherever there is wifi.

confusables.difference: Wherever is about place; whenever is about time.

entry_json.avoid: 'Wherever possible' is a useful formal phrase. Do not write 'in wherever possible'.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce two or more possibilities, or to report a yes-or-no question
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The real question is whether cities can grow without generating still more traffic.
example_sentences: I am not sure whether the office is open on Saturdays.
The decision depends on whether funding is renewed.

contexts.text: The real question is whether cities can grow without generating still more traffic.
I can't decide whether to stay another year or move back home.
The study examines whether class size affects attainment.

confusables.difference: If and whether are interchangeable in many reported questions, but only whether can follow a preposition or come before 'to'.
minimal_pair: It depends on whether he comes.
I do not know if he is coming.

confusables.difference: Whether and weather sound identical. Weather is rain and sun; whether introduces alternatives.

entry_json.avoid: After a preposition, always use whether: 'the question of whether', never 'the question of if'.

entry_json.definition: to speak very quietly so that only the person near you can hear
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Librarians spend less time asking people to whisper than they did before headphones.
example_sentences: She whispered something to the person beside her.
He whispered that the meeting had already started.

contexts.text: Librarians spend less time asking people to whisper than they did before headphones.
My friend whispered the answer to me and we both got caught.
Participants were asked to whisper rather than speak aloud during the test.

confusables.difference: Murmur is a low continuous sound and can be many voices together. Whisper is deliberately quiet speech to one person.
minimal_pair: A murmur ran through the hall.

confusables.difference: Mutter suggests complaint spoken unclearly; whisper is simply quiet.

entry_json.avoid: Whisper takes 'to' before the listener: whisper to someone, not whisper someone.

entry_json.definition: the object form of 'who', used in formal English and after prepositions
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report does not say to whom the recommendations were addressed.
example_sentences: The candidate whom the panel selected withdrew a week later.
To whom should I send the completed form?

contexts.text: The report does not say to whom the recommendations were addressed.
The person whom I spoke to was extremely helpful, actually.
Participants, most of whom were graduates, completed the survey online.

confusables.difference: Who is the subject: who wrote this? Whom is the object: to whom did you write? In speech, who is normal in both roles.
That can replace whom in defining relative clauses and is far more natural in speech.

entry_json.avoid: Whom sounds stiff in Speaking. Use it in Writing after a preposition, and after quantifiers such as 'many of whom'.

entry_json.definition: by or among many people; over a large area
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is widely accepted that early intervention is cheaper than later treatment.
example_sentences: The technique is now widely used in hospitals across Europe.
Opinions vary widely on how the money should be spent.

contexts.text: It is widely accepted that early intervention is cheaper than later treatment.
That app is widely used among students here, apparently.
The findings have been widely replicated in subsequent studies.

confusables.difference: Broadly means in general terms, without detail. Widely means among many people or across a large area.
minimal_pair: Broadly speaking, the trend is upward.

confusables.difference: Wide is the adjective for physical breadth; widely is the adverb for extent of use or spread.

entry_json.avoid: 'It is widely believed that' is a useful hedge in Task 2, but do not use it to avoid naming actual evidence.

entry_json.definition: animals and plants that live in natural conditions, not kept by people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Roads fragment habitats, and wildlife pays the price long before people notice.
example_sentences: The reserve protects wildlife across four hundred hectares.
Light pollution disturbs wildlife far beyond the edge of the city.

contexts.text: Roads fragment habitats, and wildlife pays the price long before people notice.
There's surprising wildlife in my city — foxes, mostly.
Wildlife populations declined by an average of two thirds between 1970 and 2018.

confusables.difference: Nature is everything in the natural world, including landscape and weather. Wildlife is only the living creatures and plants.
minimal_pair: I love being out in nature.
The area is rich in wildlife.

confusables.difference: Animals excludes plants; wildlife includes both, and only the wild ones.

entry_json.avoid: Wildlife is uncountable and takes a singular verb: 'wildlife is threatened', not 'are'.

entry_json.definition: ready and happy to do something if it is needed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: People are willing to recycle, but only when the system is simple enough to use without thinking.
example_sentences: Are you willing to work at weekends?
Few residents were willing to pay more for the improvement.

contexts.text: People are willing to recycle, but only when the system is simple enough to use without thinking.
I'd be willing to move abroad for the right job.
Respondents were willing to accept longer waits in return for lower costs.

confusables.difference: Ready means prepared and able to start now. Willing means you agree to do it, whether or not you are prepared.
Keen means enthusiastic. Willing only means you will not refuse.

entry_json.avoid: Willing is always followed by 'to' plus a verb. 'Willing for doing' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: one of the parts of a bird, insect or aircraft that it uses to fly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Aircraft wings are now designed to bend considerably, which improves fuel efficiency.
example_sentences: The bird had an injured wing and could not fly.
I always ask for a seat behind the wing.

contexts.text: Aircraft wings are now designed to bend considerably, which improves fuel efficiency.
I like sitting by the window, but not right over the wing.
Wing design accounts for a substantial share of fuel savings in newer aircraft.

confusables.difference: Fins are on fish and are used for swimming. Wings are for flying.
minimal_pair: The fish has a damaged fin.
The bird has a damaged wing.

entry_json.avoid: 'The left wing' and 'the right wing' also refer to politics. Context must make the sense clear.

entry_json.definition: thin metal thread, used for carrying electricity or for fastening things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Copper wire remains valuable enough that theft from railway lines is a persistent problem.
example_sentences: A loose wire was the cause of the fire.
The fence is made of wire stretched between wooden posts.

contexts.text: Copper wire remains valuable enough that theft from railway lines is a persistent problem.
There are wires all over my desk and I keep meaning to sort them out.
Copper wire remains the standard medium for local electrical distribution.

confusables.difference: A cable is thick, often several wires inside a protective cover. A wire is a single thin strand.
minimal_pair: The cable runs under the road.

confusables.difference: A cord is a flexible cable attached to an appliance; wire is the metal itself.

entry_json.avoid: Wire is uncountable when it means the material: 'a piece of wire', or 'wire fencing'.

entry_json.definition: able to make sensible decisions because of experience and good judgement
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It would be wise to test the scheme in one district before rolling it out nationally.
example_sentences: It is wise to keep a copy of every document you submit.
She was a wise and patient teacher.

contexts.text: It would be wise to test the scheme in one district before rolling it out nationally.
My grandfather gave me some very wise advice about money.
It would be wise to interpret the early results with caution.

confusables.difference: Clever is about quick thinking and ability. Wise is about good judgement built from experience, which is not the same thing.
Sensible is practical good judgement in ordinary situations. Wise suggests depth and experience.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'wise' as an ending meaning 'regarding', as in 'money-wise', in formal writing.

entry_json.definition: inside a particular period of time, distance or limit
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most complaints are resolved within ten working days, according to the published figures.
example_sentences: The shop is within walking distance of the station.
Emissions must fall by a quarter within the decade.

contexts.text: Most complaints are resolved within ten working days, according to the published figures.
Everything I need is within walking distance, which is why I chose the flat.
Symptoms usually resolve within seventy-two hours.

confusables.difference: In a week can mean after a week has passed. Within a week means at some point before the week ends, which is more precise.
minimal_pair: I will call in a week.
I will call within a week.

confusables.difference: Inside is physical position. Within is used for time limits, distances and boundaries of a system.

entry_json.avoid: Within is precise about deadlines. Do not use it loosely as a formal substitute for 'in' when describing location.

entry_json.definition: a person who sees something happen and can describe it afterwards, especially in court
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A case that depends on a single witness is far weaker than one supported by records.
example_sentences: Police are appealing for witnesses to the accident.
The witness gave evidence for over an hour.

contexts.text: A case that depends on a single witness is far weaker than one supported by records.
I was a witness to a minor crash once and had to give a statement.
Witness testimony is known to be less reliable than jurors typically assume.

confusables.difference: A spectator watches an event for pleasure. A witness sees something that matters legally.
A victim is harmed by the event; a witness only sees it.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'a witness to an accident', not 'a witness of an accident'.

entry_json.definition: to think about something because you want to know more about it, or are not certain
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Readers may wonder why the figures for 2015 are missing from the table.
example_sentences: I wonder whether the course will run again next year.
She wondered how the family had managed for so long.

contexts.text: Readers may wonder why the figures for 2015 are missing from the table.
I sometimes wonder what would have happened if I'd studied something else.
One might reasonably wonder whether the sample is representative.

confusables.difference: Wonder is about thinking. Wander means to walk without a fixed direction. The spellings are one letter apart.
minimal_pair: We wandered through the old town.

confusables.difference: Think can be a settled opinion. Wonder always contains uncertainty and a question.

entry_json.avoid: 'I wonder if you could help me' is a polite request, not a real question about your thoughts.

entry_json.definition: the soft thick hair of sheep, or the thread and cloth made from it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wool takes far more water to produce than synthetic fibre, but it lasts much longer.
example_sentences: She was wearing a heavy wool coat.
The scarf is pure wool and surprisingly warm.

contexts.text: Wool takes far more water to produce than synthetic fibre, but it lasts much longer.
I've had the same wool jumper for about ten years.
Wool exports formed the basis of the regional economy until the 1960s.

confusables.difference: Cotton comes from a plant and is light and cool. Wool comes from sheep and is warm.
Wool is the noun; woollen is the adjective. Both 'a wool coat' and 'a woollen coat' are used.

entry_json.avoid: Note the pronunciation: /wʊl/, a short vowel like 'put', not like 'cool'.

entry_json.definition: existing or happening in all parts of the world
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Worldwide demand for lithium has grown faster than any supplier predicted.
example_sentences: The company has a worldwide network of suppliers.
There is worldwide concern about antibiotic resistance.

contexts.text: Worldwide demand for lithium has grown faster than any supplier predicted.
That band has a worldwide following, apparently, though I'd never heard of them.
Worldwide emissions rose in every year of the period except 2020.

confusables.difference: Global and worldwide are close synonyms. Global is more common in academic writing; worldwide is slightly more commercial.
International means between countries. Worldwide means in all of them.

entry_json.avoid: As an adverb it is also 'worldwide': 'sales rose worldwide'. Do not write 'worldwidely'.

entry_json.definition: having a particular value, or good enough to justify the time or money spent
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A short course in academic writing is worth more to most candidates than another practice test.
example_sentences: The house is worth about three hundred thousand pounds.
It is worth checking the timetable before you leave.

contexts.text: A short course in academic writing is worth more to most candidates than another practice test.
The trip was expensive but honestly it was worth every penny.
It is worth noting that the sample excluded part-time employees.

confusables.difference: Valuable is an adjective used before a noun or after 'be'. Worth needs an amount or an -ing form after it.
minimal_pair: The painting is worth a fortune.

confusables.difference: Worthy means deserving respect and is quite different: 'a worthy cause', not 'a worth cause'.

entry_json.avoid: Worth is followed by the -ing form, never the infinitive: 'worth visiting', not 'worth to visit'.

entry_json.definition: an injury to the body in which the skin is cut or broken
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Infected wounds account for a large share of hospital readmissions after surgery.
example_sentences: The wound took three weeks to heal completely.
Clean the wound thoroughly before covering it.

contexts.text: Infected wounds account for a large share of hospital readmissions after surgery.
The wound on my hand healed quickly, luckily.
Wound infection rates fell after the new protocol was introduced.

confusables.difference: Injury is the general word for any harm to the body, including broken bones. A wound specifically breaks the skin.
minimal_pair: He suffered a deep wound to the arm.

confusables.difference: A scar is the mark left after a wound heals.

entry_json.avoid: This noun is /wuːnd/, rhyming with 'spooned'. The past tense of 'wind' is spelled the same but said /waʊnd/.

entry_json.definition: to cover something completely by folding paper or material around it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Supermarkets wrap fresh produce in plastic that adds days of shelf life and centuries of waste.
example_sentences: She wrapped the present in brown paper.
Wrap the sandwiches so they do not dry out.

contexts.text: Supermarkets wrap fresh produce in plastic that adds days of shelf life and centuries of waste.
I wrap my lunch in a cloth now instead of using foil.
Produce wrapped in plastic film generates significant unnecessary waste.

confusables.difference: Cover means putting something over the top. Wrap means folding material all the way round.
minimal_pair: Cover the pan with a lid.

confusables.difference: Pack means putting things into a container; wrap means enclosing one thing in material.

entry_json.avoid: The w is silent: /ræp/, exactly like 'rap'. Double the p before endings: wrapped, wrapping.

entry_json.definition: expressed in writing rather than in speech
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Written English is more tolerant of long sentences than spoken English ever is.
example_sentences: You will receive written confirmation within five working days.
The test has a written section and an oral one.

contexts.text: Written English is more tolerant of long sentences than spoken English ever is.
I got written confirmation by email, so at least I have a record.
Written responses were coded independently by two researchers.

confusables.difference: Written and spoken are the standard pair for describing language. Use both when comparing the two skills.
Writing is the noun and the activity. Written is the adjective placed before a noun.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'a writing agreement'. The adjective is written.

entry_json.definition: an area of hard ground next to a building; or a unit of length equal to about 0.91 metres
entry_json.own_context_sentence: School yards covered in tarmac heat up far faster than those with any planting.
example_sentences: The children play in the school yard at lunchtime.
The fabric is sold by the yard in that shop.

contexts.text: School yards covered in tarmac heat up far faster than those with any planting.
We used to play football in the yard behind the flats.
Yard surfaces contribute measurably to the urban heat island effect.

confusables.difference: In British English a garden has grass and plants. A yard is hard ground, often for work or play.
minimal_pair: The tools are in the yard.

confusables.difference: A yard is slightly less than a metre. Do not use the two interchangeably in data.

entry_json.avoid: In American English 'yard' means what British English calls a garden. With British examiners, keep them separate.

entry_json.definition: the period of life when someone is young; or young people considered as a group
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Youth unemployment is the single clearest warning sign of an economy in trouble.
example_sentences: He spent his youth in a small fishing town.
The centre runs sports programmes for local youth.

contexts.text: Youth unemployment is the single clearest warning sign of an economy in trouble.
In my youth I never imagined I'd live in another country.
Youth participation in voting has risen in each of the last three elections.

confusables.difference: Childhood is roughly up to twelve. Youth covers the teenage years and early twenties.
minimal_pair: He was ambitious in his youth.

confusables.difference: 'Young people' is the natural plural in most sentences. 'Youths' can sound negative in British news writing.

entry_json.avoid: Prefer 'young people' to 'youths' in essays. 'Youths' often carries a suggestion of trouble.

entry_json.definition: an area that is different from those around it because of a particular purpose or quality
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cities that create low-emission zones see traffic fall in them and rise just outside.
example_sentences: Parking is not permitted in this zone.
The building sits in a zone at high risk of flooding.

contexts.text: Cities that create low-emission zones see traffic fall in them and rise just outside.
The centre is a pedestrian zone now, which makes it much nicer to walk around.
Properties within the flood zone have become substantially harder to insure.

confusables.difference: Area is the general word for any part of a place. A zone has been marked out deliberately for a purpose.
A region is a large geographical division of a country. A zone is usually smaller and defined by rules.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'zone' only where there is a real boundary or rule. Otherwise 'area' is more accurate.
